newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Orange see more Britons on mobiles.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Orange see more Britons on mobiles.

text.p: Orange Plc, Britain's youngest mobile telephone operator, said on Tuesday it expected at least 20 percent of Britons to use mobile phones by the year 2000.

Mobile penetration in Britain was around 11.7 percent at the end of last year, but Orange's managing director Hans Snook told Reuters that he saw no difficulty in raising that level -- possibly to as much as 40 percent.
"I don't see any difficulty at all that by the year 2000, penetration in the UK will be 20 percent," he said.
"Scandinavian countries now have about 30 percent penetration and are growing, Australia has about 25 percent, U.S. has 17 percent and we're sitting here with 11/12 percent -- it's silly.
"A lot of people are now predicting 40 percent penetration 10 years from now and I think that looks very do-able."
The loss-making company, which was floated last March at 205 pence per share, initially saw its stock slump to 157.5p before recovering over the last few weeks to trade at 218p on Tuesday.

Fears that a sharp drop in the growth of subscriber numbers was pointing to a permanent slow-down hit Britain's four mobile operators but were assuaged when subscriber numbers picked up again at the end of 1996.
Orange, which earlier reported its first full year results since flotation, now has a subscriber base that tops 850,000 and gives it a 11.5 percent market share.

Snook expects the all important average retained revenue per Orange subscriber to rise from around 442 pounds per year, partly because dominant telecoms player British Telecommunications last month raised the price of a call to Orange phones from its fixed lines.
"Current incoming call revenues are about 60 stg per month. If that doubles it will add a fair chunk to average revenues for 1997," Snook said.

Orange, which reported annual pretax losses in line with analysts' expectations of 229 million stg, boasts the lowest 'churn rate' -- customers disconnecting or being excluded for bad debt or fraud -- in the industry.
At 18.6 percent, it has risen from 18.1 percent in 1995 but is still well below the industry average or 28 percent clocked up by rivals Vodafone Group Plc, Cellnet and One-2-One.

Some analysts put this down to tighter credit controls, although Snook says customers are satisfied with the service and over 80 percent had recommended to it friends. "We're doing a lot of right things," he said.
The company, which plans to cover 96 percent of the UK population by the end of the year, is also hoping to win a mobile licence in Greece and the Netherlands.
Despite companies from more than 25 countries contacting Orange about forming local partnerships, Snook said other overseas expansion projects were on the back burner.

Backed by main shareholder Hong Kong conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa, Orange is hoping to be the chosen partner to take a 30 percent stake in the cellular arm of Greek national operator OTE this month.
"We have an arrangement with Hutchison Whampoa for the financing that gives really pure upside to Orange investors if we get it," Snook said.
The amount of investment put up by the Hong Kong conglomerate for the deal remain a commercial secret.
Orange raised 1.2 billion stg via a debt facility in December 1995 for its UK expansion plans, and since then, has withdrawn about 785 million stg.
Meantime, Orange says it is ahead of its rivals in plans to introduce by April or May dual band handsets that operate at both 1800 and 900 MHz.
Customers will be able to make calls in more than 50 countries by the end of the year using the handsets developed by Motorola.
-- Kirstin Ridley, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7987
